steps.body: Time to settle arguments. When two fractions share a bottom, their pieces are the **same size** — so comparing is just counting. 5/8 vs 3/8 of one cake is five pieces against three of the exact same piece. The tops settle it.

widget.prompt: Order these from SMALLEST to biggest — all pieces are sevenths of the same bar.

misorderFeedback.feedback: Same-size pieces — three of them stack lower than five. 3/7 stands before 5/7.
Six sevenths beats five — with matching pieces, the bigger count is the bigger amount.

widget.missFeedback: Every one is built from sevenths — so the TOP alone sets the order.
widget.successFeedback: 2/7, 3/7, 5/7, 6/7 — matching pieces, rising counts, rising amounts.

predict.prompt: All pieces are sevenths of the SAME bar. Predict: what settles which stack is biggest?

options.label: How many sevenths — the top number
You can't tell without a picture

predict.reveal: Matching bottoms mean matching piece sizes — so ordering sevenths is pure counting. The top number settles it, and the bars will show exactly that.

explanationVariants: Same cake, same piece size (eighths) — five pieces simply beat three.
On the line: same jump size, and 5/8 takes two more jumps than 3/8, landing farther out.

widget.prompt: Which is more of the same cake: 3/8 or 5/8?
widget.leftFeedback: Both fractions use eighth-size pieces. With piece size equal, MORE pieces is more cake: 5 beats 3.
widget.equalFeedback: The bottoms match, but the tops don't — that two-piece gap is real cake.
widget.successFeedback: Matching eighth-pieces — and five of them beat three.

steps.body: See it both ways. **On the line:** same bottoms mean same jump size — the bigger top takes more jumps and lands farther from 0. **On the bar:** more same-size pieces stack higher. Either picture, the count carries the day.

explanationVariants: Same-size sandwiches, same-size pieces: Ben's 5 sixths beat Ana's 4 by exactly one sixth-piece.
Their leftovers tell the same story: Ana left 2/6, Ben left 1/6 — one piece apart either way.

widget.prompt: Ana ate 4/6 of her sandwich; Ben ate 5/6 of his. The sandwiches are the same size. How many MORE sixths did Ben eat?

commonErrors.feedback: 9 ADDED their counts. 'How many more' measures the gap between them: 5 − 4.
5 is Ben's whole count. The question asks how far AHEAD of Ana he is — subtract her 4.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Same-size pieces, so just compare counts: 5 − 4.

widget.prompt: Tap EVERY fraction that is bigger than 3/5.

hotspots.feedback: Two fifths falls SHORT of three — same pieces, smaller count.
A single fifth is the smallest of the bunch — two pieces below the 3/5 bar.

widget.missFeedback: All fifths — so compare each top to 3.
widget.successFeedback: 4/5 and 5/5 (the whole bar!) clear the 3/5 bar; 1/5 and 2/5 fall short.

cml.actionGoal: Manipulate the model and track how it represents compare same denom.
invariants: The manipulated model and the mathematical relationship for compare same denom must stay consistent.
misconceptions: Changing a visible feature without preserving the relationship that defines compare same denom.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: What change would make the model stop representing the same mathematical relationship?

steps.body: But WHY does the top settle it?
explanationVariants: Matching bottoms guarantee matching piece sizes — and counting only compares fairly when the things counted are the same size.
It's like coins: five dimes beat three dimes because dimes match. Five dimes vs three quarters is a different game.

widget.prompt: Why can the TOPS settle it when the bottoms match?

options.label: Matching bottoms mean matching piece sizes — so more pieces really is more
options.feedback: Counting compares fairly only when the counted things match — and matching bottoms guarantee it.

options.label: The top number always settles every comparison
options.feedback: Careful — only when the piece sizes match! 2/3 vs 2/8 has matching TOPS, and the next lesson shows the top settles nothing there.

options.label: Bigger numbers always win in math
options.feedback: The bottom number already broke that rule once (1/8 < 1/3). Here it's the matching piece size, not bigness, doing the work.

options.label: It can't — you always need a picture
options.feedback: Pictures never hurt, but matching bottoms make the shortcut safe: same pieces, so the count decides.

hints: Both teams run legs of the SAME trail — tenths all around.
Red has 7 tenths behind it, Blue has 4.
'How many more' is the gap between the counts.
explanationVariants: Same-size legs, so the gap is pure counting: 7 − 4 = 3 tenths of the trail.
Line view: both teams jump in tenths; Red stands 3 jumps farther along.

widget.prompt: A relay trail is split into 10 equal legs. Team Red has finished 7 legs; Team Blue has finished 4. How many more TENTHS of the trail has Red covered?

commonErrors.feedback: 11 added the two teams — but they're racing, not pooling. The gap between 7 and 4 legs is what's asked.
7 is Red's full count. 'How many MORE' compares it to Blue's 4: subtract.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Equal legs make it a counting gap: 7 − 4.

takeaways: Same bottoms = same piece size, so the tops settle it by counting.
On the line: same jump size, more jumps lands farther.
The shortcut is safe ONLY because the pieces match.
steps.teaser: next: the tables turn — same TOPS, different bottoms, and counting stops working.

concept.body: Quick rewind. Same bottoms are like **same coins**: comparing 7 dimes to 4 dimes is just counting dimes. Sevenths against sevenths, eighths against eighths — match the pieces, then count.

explanationVariants: Both are ninths — same piece size — and seven pieces beat two.

widget.prompt: Which is more of the same pie: 2/9 or 7/9?

options.feedback: Both use ninth-size pieces — with sizes matching, the bigger count (7) is the bigger amount.

options.label: They're equal
options.feedback: The bottoms match but the tops sit five pieces apart — a real gap of pie.
